title: Fixture: two episodes of predictive control
plan_sentence: Over two episodes we see why predictive control is stable and then shrink its window to nothing, on a ball balanced on a hilltop.
playlist_description: Fixture series for the tests: two episodes adapted from a curator plan.

episodes.title: Why predictive control is stable: the cost still to pay
episodes.hook: A predictive controller plans a few steps ahead, takes only the first step, and throws the rest of the plan away. Then it plans again from wherever it landed. Why should that ever settle down? The answer is a number the controller computes anyway: the cost still to pay. And you'll see a controller that converges every time while the textbook proof of its stability fails at every step.

the boundary term W paid at the end of the window

if W falls along a reference motion at least as fast as cost is spent, V_N falls by at least each step's cost
the shifted plan stays feasible
with the usual bounds the target is asymptotically stable
the proof never used the window length N
with the step's cost computed exactly, V_1 = W and the drop equals the step cost (N = 1, the toy)

episodes.story_beat: Proves in five lines why a receding-window controller with a boundary term and a terminal region is stable; says what the window length does and does not change; explains why a convergent controller can still fail its certificate.

takeaway.sentence: The cost still to pay falls by at least the cost of each step, provided the boundary term pays for the tail; that certificate belongs to the pair of step cost and boundary term, not to the controller.

series_context.spoken: This is the first of two episodes in The Mechanics of Predictive Control, and it starts from scratch. Over five episodes, we'll see why predictive control is stable, shrink its planning window down to nothing, find momenta hiding inside its optimizer, and then test all of it on a two-link robot arm: first with a window of length zero, then with real ones.

outline.beat: Hook, series context and the spoken plan of the series

The receding window, named: window of N steps, terminal region, boundary term W, first step applied; cost per step = Lagrangian, total = action, least cost still to pay = remaining action V_N (four-row MPC-to-mechanics dictionary)

Why it falls: yesterday's plan minus the step taken, plus one reference step inside the region, is a valid plan today; if W falls along the reference motion at least as fast as cost is spent, V_N(q+) - V_N(q) <= -L_d(q,q+); the plan stays feasible; with the usual bounds, asymptotic stability

What the window length does: the proof never used N; a longer window enlarges the set of starting points and lowers V_N; with an exact boundary term the total stays 0.5 while the split between computed window and estimated tail moves
One step, exactly: N = 1 on the toy L = v^2/2 + q^2/2, h = 0.1, W = q^2/2; with the step's cost computed exactly, V_1 = W and the drop equals the step cost at every step (q shrinks by e^-0.1)

The paradox resolved: rectangle-rule step cost, same W: q -> 0.909 q converges, but V_1 > W and the drop 0.0876 is less than the step cost 0.0913, at every step; inflate W by 20 % (threshold 1.051) and every inequality holds: the certificate belongs to the pair

episodes.title: The hilltop: Hamilton–Jacobi and the stable manifold
episodes.hook: Here is a ball on a hill. I want it to stay on top: not held there, but arriving there, rolling, and stopping exactly on the summit. Of all the ways to push it, only one works. By the end of this video you will see what finds that one push: the remaining action, the cost still to be paid from here on.

ideas.text: the cost read as kinetic minus potential energy on a hilltop
the one curve of pushes that arrives at the summit
the momentum p = -V'
the energy H(q, p), zero on the arriving curve
only the zero-energy push arrives, and the remaining action generates it: p = -V', H(q, -V') = 0
along it the remaining action falls at the rate of the cost
the Legendre transform from cost to energy
shrinking the window: W is certified wherever H(q, -grad W) >= 0
W = cV is certified for c >= 1
a speed limit changes which boundary term is exact

episodes.story_beat: Derives the certificate H(q, -grad W) >= 0 by shrinking the window; sees on a phase portrait why only the zero-energy push arrives; reads the cost still to pay as the generator of that push; sees that a speed limit changes which boundary term is exact.

takeaway.sentence: The cost still to pay generates the momentum, solves the Hamilton–Jacobi equation at zero energy and falls at exactly the rate of the cost; a boundary term W is certified wherever H(q, -grad W) is at least zero.

series_context.spoken: This is episode two of two in The Mechanics of Predictive Control. It builds on the first episode, on why predictive control is stable. If you're joining here, welcome: that result takes forty seconds to restate.

recap.title: Recap: why predictive control is stable
recap.restates: A predictive controller plans over a window, pays a boundary term W at its end, applies the first step and repeats. The least cost still to pay then drops after each step by at least that step's cost, provided W drops at least as fast as cost is spent near the target; in continuous time, W-dot at most minus L. The requirement belongs to the pair of cost and boundary term: a controller can converge while a badly matched W fails to certify it.

outline.beat: Series context with the builds-on frame; Recap: why predictive control is stable
A ball on a hilltop: the cost read as kinetic minus potential energy; Newton's law on an inverted parabola; true minima (no conjugate point)
Only one push arrives: saddle in the (q, p) plane, three pushes, the stable manifold; V generates it: p = -V', H(q, -V') = 0, integral of L = V
Shrinking the window: the bracket L + grad W . v, Legendre transform, the certificate H(q, -grad W) >= 0; one minimization, two outputs; scaled candidates W = cV
A finite window and the role of the boundary term; Adding a speed limit (clipped law, constrained remaining action); Why the cost of motion stays
Three facts about V; outro with the takeaway card and teaser
